title: Grade 9 English — Direct & Indirect Speech and Vocabulary
description: Direct and Indirect Speech and Vocabulary practice questions
subject: english

questions.question: Change to indirect speech: Ram said, 'I am happy.'
options: Ram said that he is happy.
Ram said that he was happy.
Ram says that he was happy.
Ram told that I am happy.
questions.explanation: In indirect speech (past reporting verb 'said'), present tense shifts to past: 'am' → 'was'. Pronoun 'I' shifts to 'he'. Use 'that' as conjunction.

questions.question: Change to indirect speech: She said, 'I will come tomorrow.'
options: She said that she would come the next day.
She said that she will come tomorrow.
She says that she would come tomorrow.
She told that she will come the next day.
questions.explanation: In indirect speech: 'will' → 'would'; 'tomorrow' → 'the next day'. Also 'I' → 'she'. Use 'said that'.

questions.question: Which tense change is correct in indirect speech?
questions.explanation: Tense backshift in indirect speech: Simple present (am/is/are) → Simple past (was/were). All tenses shift one step back in time.

questions.question: Change to direct speech: He asked me if I liked music.
questions.explanation: Indirect question with 'if' → Direct speech with yes/no question. 'if I liked' → 'Do you like?' (past → present, 'I' becomes 'you').

questions.question: When reporting commands/requests, we use:
questions.explanation: Commands and requests in indirect speech: told/asked + object + to + infinitive. Example: 'Come here' → He told me to come there.

questions.question: Change to indirect speech: The teacher said, 'The Earth revolves around the Sun.'
options: The teacher said that the Earth revolved around the Sun.
The teacher said that the Earth revolves around the Sun.
The teacher told that the Earth revolves around the Sun.
The teacher said that the Earth will revolve around the Sun.
questions.explanation: Universal truths and scientific facts do NOT undergo tense change in indirect speech. 'revolves' remains in present tense.

questions.question: In indirect speech, 'this' changes to:
questions.explanation: Time and place expressions change in indirect speech: this → that, these → those, here → there, now → then, today → that day.

questions.question: Change to indirect speech: He said to me, 'Please help me.'
options: He said to me to please help him.
He requested me to help him.
He told me that please help him.
He asked me that help him.
questions.explanation: Polite requests with 'please' use 'requested'. 'He requested me to help him.' — note 'me' stays as object, 'me' in the original becomes 'him'.

questions.question: The synonym of 'magnanimous' is:
questions.explanation: Magnanimous means generously forgiving or big-hearted. Synonym: generous, benevolent, noble. Antonym: petty, mean.

questions.question: The antonym of 'diligent' is:
questions.explanation: Diligent means showing steady effort and care. Its antonym is lazy (indolent, idle).

questions.question: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom 'break the ice':
options: To start a conversation in a social situation
questions.explanation: 'Break the ice' means to do or say something to relieve tension and start a conversation or interaction, especially among strangers.

questions.question: The word 'ambiguous' means:
options: Open to more than one interpretation
questions.explanation: Ambiguous: having more than one possible meaning; unclear. Example: 'I saw the man with binoculars' — who has the binoculars?

questions.question: Choose the correct spelling:
questions.explanation: 'Occasion' is the correct spelling. Common error: double-c and single-s (occ-as-ion).

questions.question: The prefix 'mis-' in 'misunderstand' means:
questions.explanation: The prefix 'mis-' means wrongly or badly. Misunderstand = understand wrongly. Other examples: mislead, misbehave, misconduct.

questions.question: What is the meaning of the idiom 'a blessing in disguise'?
options: Something that seems bad but turns out to be good
questions.explanation: 'A blessing in disguise' means an apparent misfortune that eventually has a good outcome. Example: Missing the bus was a blessing in disguise — I met my old friend at the stop.
